records.sourceFile: Hamstring strength assessment methods in sport - A systematic review and meta-analysis of post-activity strength decrements, asymmetry benchmarks, and measurement reliability.pdf

paper.citation: Sundh AE, Ripley NJ, Lamb AJ, Comfort P. Hamstring strength assessment methods in sport: A systematic review and meta-analysis of post-activity strength decrements, asymmetry benchmarks, and measurement reliability. PLoS One. 2026;21(7):e0352509.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis examined hamstring strength tests used in sport. Isokinetic dynamometry, force platforms and Nordic devices were the main methods, and the authors report that strength deficits persisted for 24 to 72 hours after on-field activity. Limb-to-limb asymmetry was about 3 to 4 percent, which the authors describe as normative.
paper.tldr: Hamstring strength tests on isokinetic, force plate and Nordic devices are generally reliable, and strength stays lower for about 24 to 72 hours after on-field activity. Use each athlete's own baseline, and check that any change or limb difference is larger than the test's measurement error before acting on it.
paper.methods: PRISMA 2020 systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42025571001) of PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science to 1 November 2025, with quality scored on a 12-item modified Downs and Black checklist. Random-effects meta-analyses (REML) pooled strength change at immediate, 24, 48 and 72 hour time points, and separately pooled limb-to-limb differences from 77 studies.
paper.findings: 161 studies were included (106 in quantitative analysis) and none was rated poor quality. Pooled post-activity effects were -0.66 immediately, -0.67 at 24 hours, -0.52 at 48 hours and -0.40 at 72 hours, with 95% confidence intervals below zero and low heterogeneity. The weighted limb difference was 2.6% directional and 3.5% non-directional, and reliability was described as generally acceptable to good, with concentric peak torque more reliable than eccentric and rapid force measures less reliable than peak force.
paper.limitations: Section 3.6 describes reliability as generally acceptable to moderate, while the abstract and discussion say good, and SEM and MDD were reported in few studies. The concentric subgroups rest on 2 studies, the 24-hour contraction-mode difference (p = 0.04) is fragile, and the Egger tests were underpowered. Data extraction was done by one reviewer, no certainty-of-evidence rating was applied, and the sample was 78% male.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose a hamstring test the staff can run consistently and record its SEM or MDD so that changes can be judged against measurement noise. Plan around the reported 24 to 72 hour window of lower strength after on-field activity, and compare each athlete with their own baseline. Read limb differences of about 3 to 4 percent as typical for healthy athletes, and act only when an individual's difference clearly exceeds the test's error.
paper.athleteDev: Use one test protocol per athlete as a baseline, and compare post-session or post-game values with that baseline rather than with group norms. The authors observed broadly similar post-activity decrements across devices, though the meta-analysis only compared contraction modes, so device choice can follow resources and access but is not shown to be interchangeable. Rapid force (RFD) measures were less reliable than peak force, so interpret them with caution.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included only healthy athletes with no lower-limb injury in the prior 6 months, so its asymmetry benchmarks, reliability values and post-activity decrements are not criteria for clearing a hamstring injury.

records.sourceFile: Role of video review for sport-related concussion identification - a systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Townsend DC, Saker A, Scandrett K, Green M, Brownlow M, Riley P, et al. Role of video review for sport-related concussion identification: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2025.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of the frequency and diagnostic accuracy of visible signs of sport-related concussion identified through video review, and of the role of injury mechanism. Of 29 included studies, most visible signs showed low sensitivity and high specificity, and only two studies included female athletes.
paper.tldr: Visible signs on video are useful prompts to remove and assess a player, but most miss more than half of concussions and about a quarter of concussions show no sign at all. Video review should support, not replace, a full multimodal sideline assessment.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA for diagnostic test accuracy, not preregistered, searching MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library from 1 January 2001, with the search updated to June 2024. Peer-reviewed English studies using clinical diagnosis or a consensus definition of concussion as reference were included; risk of bias used QUADAS-2, and summary sensitivity and specificity per visible sign were estimated with bivariate random-effects models where data allowed.
paper.findings: The most frequent signs were 'slow to get up' (37.6%) and 'motor incoordination' (26.7%), and no visible sign was seen in 23.6% of concussions. Summary sensitivity was low for most signs (for example lying motionless 0.20, motor incoordination 0.32, impact seizure 0.05) with high specificity (0.91 to 1.00), while 'slow to get up' had sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.27. Expert raters generally agreed more than novices, though expert kappa values ranged from 0.08 to 0.89, and high impact speed, direct head contact with a solid object and foul play increased the likelihood of a concussion diagnosis.
paper.limitations: Only eight of 29 studies had low risk of bias, most were retrospective, and rater blinding was often unreported. Visible sign definitions varied, which introduces error into summary estimates, and the evidence comes mainly from male professional sport where multi-angle footage is available. The review was funded by the Premier League and several authors were Premier League employees or consultants.
paper.practicalImplications: A visible sign on video is a reason to remove and assess the player, but its absence does not rule out concussion, and 'slow to get up' is sensitive but not specific. Expert reviewers and standard sign definitions improve reliability, and video should feed into a multimodal assessment rather than stand alone.
paper.athleteDev: Cannot inform performance work. For medical staff using video, it supports trained reviewers and treating video as a prompt for clinical assessment rather than a decision tool.
paper.rtp: Relevant to concussion identification and removal from play, not to return-to-play progression or clearance. A negative video review cannot rule out concussion, so it should not shortcut the clinical assessment.

records.sourceFile: Acute-chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports - a multilevel meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Ding L, Weldon A, Xu J, Malone S, Sampaio J, Zhang Z, et al. Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1896651.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the association between acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk in team-sport athletes. Of 41 eligible studies, 16 (797 athletes) were pooled, showing a small-to-moderate association with injury (g = 0.35) and very high heterogeneity.
paper.tldr: In team-sport athletes, a high acute:chronic workload ratio was associated with somewhat higher injury risk, most clearly for contact and non-contact injuries. The authors conclude it is a contextual monitoring flag within a multi-marker load-management approach, not a stand-alone predictor or threshold.
paper.methods: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to 28 October 2024, with supplementary Google Scholar, ResearchGate and reference-list searches; English only. Cohort studies (prospective or retrospective), trials and other longitudinal studies of competitive team-sport athletes reporting ACWR and injury were eligible; effect sizes were converted to Hedges g and pooled with a three-level random-effects model, with moderator analyses, Newcastle-Ottawa quality ratings and Egger and trim-and-fill tests. Registered in PROSPERO (CRD420245127618).
paper.findings: Elevated ACWR was associated with higher injury risk (g = 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.54, p < 0.001; I2 = 95.8%). Injury type was the only significant moderator: contact (g = 0.54) and non-contact injuries (g = 0.55) showed similar associations, while time-loss injuries showed a near-null effect (g = 0.01, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.37). Load type, calculation method (rolling average vs EWMA), time window and sport type were not significant moderators, and leave-one-out estimates ranged from 0.33 to 0.37.
paper.limitations: Residual statistical dependence may remain when several outcomes, time windows or workload metrics come from the same cohort, and several moderator analyses rested on few studies. Most cohort studies were of moderate quality (80%), with common problems in confounding control and follow-up reporting, and reverse causation from pre-injury training changes cannot be ruled out. The search was English only with no grey literature, the abstract says prospective designs while the methods also allow retrospective cohorts, and PROSPERO registration (18 August 2025) postdates the search, while the printed ID (CRD420245127618) looks inconsistent with that date.
paper.practicalImplications: Use ACWR as a contextual flag that prompts a review of workload progression, symptoms, wellness and schedule, within an individualized multi-marker load-management system. The authors state the pooled effect should not be read as a 35% increase in injury risk, and thresholds such as 0.8 to 1.3 or above 1.5 are only heuristic reference points.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can track ACWR alongside other load and wellness markers to spot unusual workload changes, but should not use it alone to decide training. The review addresses injury risk, not performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Limited relevance to return to sport: the review covers injury risk in team-sport athletes, not rehabilitation. The authors state ACWR should not be used in isolation to decide whether an athlete returns to play.
